name: Freya Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's all right. I'll be straight with you, I'm not someone who goes on about things online, so you'll get the same answer in private as in public, mostly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a cardboard box plant, on the corrugator. That's the long machine, about a hundred metres, that glues the wavy paper between two flat sheets to make the board, then cuts it to size. I'm on the wet end, so I watch the steam, the glue and the paper reels, and I splice in a new reel without stopping the line, which takes a bit of practice. Six to two, Monday to Friday. I like that it's real work and you can see the stacks at the end of the day. The heat in summer is the worst part, and the new managers who've never stood on a line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fifteen years. My husband Sam's a plumber, he runs his own small business with one apprentice. We've got Hannah, who's thirteen, and Joseph, ten. And church on Sundays, which is where most of our friends are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People who sit at desks all day get excited about computers. The rest of us have work to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be pleased. I've never used any of these AI programs and I don't want to. I don't need a computer to tell me when the glue's too thin, I can smell it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep my shifts, keep putting money by. We've got a good year of savings and the house is half paid, so we're comfortable. Maybe we'd finally redo the bathroom, Sam's been promising for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as any other Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young managers, maybe. They love a new system. They'd be disappointed and the rest of us would carry on as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has your plant changed much over the years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The plant's been bought twice since I started and each time they said everything would change. It never did, much. We still run the same corrugator, just with a newer screen.

S0.say: I'm not surprised, because people who sit at desks all day get excited about computers. The rest of us have work to do.
S0.think: I'd be pleased, because I've never used these AI programs and don't want to. I can smell when the glue's too thin without a computer.
S0.do: Keeps her shifts and keeps putting money by from a year of savings. Finally redoes the bathroom with her husband.
S0.feel: Calm, the same as any other Monday.
S0.quote: I don't need a computer to tell me when the glue's too thin, I can smell it.
S0.fieldNote: Freya is plain-speaking and proud of her craft, with a clear distrust of desk-based enthusiasm. Her calm comes from a year of savings and a half-paid house. She's seen two takeovers come and go, which makes her sceptical of promised change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have a right to run their own affairs, but they owe something to the people who built them up. Keep the apprentices, keep the experienced hands. I wouldn't post it, I'd say it after church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think they'd finally automate the reel changes. There's a machine that does splicing on its own, they showed us a video once. If they buy that, I'm on half the job I was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and wait to see what they actually do. I'd put an extra 200 a month into savings. I wouldn't go on a course unless they made me, and if they did, I'd do it, but I'd grumble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just that feeling when the weather's turning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd grumble. Would you say that to your manager, or keep it to yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably both. I'd tell the manager I'm happy to learn, and then I'd tell Sam in the car that I'm not. That's honest, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if things got rough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam, then the church. We've got people there who'd help find work, they always do. That's how it should be, family and neighbours first, not forms at the job centre.

S1.say: Businesses have a right to run their own affairs, but they owe something to the people who built them up. Keep the apprentices and the experienced hands.
S1.think: I think they'd finally automate the reel changes with a splicer that works on its own. If they buy that, I'm on half the job I was.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and waits to see what the company does. Adds 200 a month to savings and only goes on a course if required.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like the feeling when the weather's turning.
S1.quote: I'd tell the manager I'm happy to learn, and then I'd tell Sam in the car that I'm not.
S1.fieldNote: Freya respects a company's right to choose but expects loyalty in return, a very traditional bargain. She's open about the gap between what she'd tell her manager and what she'd say in the car. Family and church are her first safety net, not the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is people playing with things they don't understand, and the rest of us pay for it. I'd say it to anyone who asked, and I'd pray about it, I'm not ashamed to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think my job's done. A machine that can do anything can splice a reel. And I don't think Sam's safe either, if they've got robots that can get under a sink. I'd be frightened for the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Sam and work out what we can live on. We'd cut back hard, no holidays, no bathroom, and keep the savings for the mortgage. I'd stay at the plant till the last day. If I lost the job, I'd help Sam with his phones and bookings, as long as he still has customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at night, I know I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning mean for someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. You can't change who you are in two years. I'm forty-three, I've done one thing well for fifteen years, and two years from now somebody tells me it's worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What frightens you most for the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they'll grow up with nothing to do. Work's how you learn who you are. I'd tell them to stay close to family, because that won't change.

S2.say: This is people playing with things they don't understand, and the rest of us pay for it. I'd say it to anyone, and I'd pray about it.
S2.think: My job's done, because a machine that can do anything can splice a reel. Sam isn't safe either if robots can get under a sink, and I'd be frightened for the children.
S2.do: Works out with her husband what they can live on, cuts holidays and the bathroom, and keeps savings for the mortgage. Stays at the plant until the last day, then helps with his phones and bookings if he still has customers.
S2.quote: I'm forty-three, I've done one thing well for fifteen years, and two years from now somebody tells me it's worth nothing.
S2.fieldNote: Freya blames the people building the technology rather than the government or her employer. Her alarm is about identity as much as money: fifteen years of skill made worthless. Her fallback is family, helping in her husband's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so the companies and the councils had better plan. Apprenticeships, local jobs, that kind of thing. Not just cheques in the post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried. Five years sounds like a lot, but I know I'd spend most of it hoping it wasn't true. I'd think about Sam's business more, and Joseph, who loves following his dad around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down the mortgage, maybe 10,000 in the first year. I'd stay on the corrugator. Around year three I'd start doing Sam's paperwork properly, learning the bookings and the accounts, so I'm ready if the plant goes. I wouldn't use any AI for it, I'd do it the way Sam's mum did it, in a book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More in control than with two years, but still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do it in a book. Would you really avoid the computer entirely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, well. Maybe the accounting program. Not the AI. I'll learn a spreadsheet if I must, but I'm not asking a robot how to run my own family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Joseph?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's ten, so he'd be fifteen. I'd want him to start with Sam as soon as he can. A trade in the family is worth more than a certificate.

S3.say: There's time to plan, so the companies and councils had better plan for apprenticeships and local jobs. Not just cheques in the post.
S3.think: I'd still be worried, because I'd spend most of five years hoping it wasn't true. I'd think more about Sam's business and about Joseph.
S3.do: Pays about 10,000 off the mortgage in the first year and stays on the corrugator. Around year three takes on her husband's paperwork and bookings so she's ready if the plant goes, and steers her son towards working with his dad.
S3.feel: Anxious, more in control than with two years, but still worried.
S3.quote: I'll learn a spreadsheet if I must, but I'm not asking a robot how to run my own family.
S3.fieldNote: Five years doesn't make Freya less worried so much as more orderly. She'd accept a spreadsheet but draws a firm line at AI, tying it to running her own family. A family trade passed to Joseph is her picture of security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough to do things properly: keep the apprenticeships going, keep families together. I'd want our church and our town to plan for it, not wait for the government to send someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years gets me to fifty-three, and I think I'd see it through at the plant. But I'd still be uneasy about the end of it. Even with time, the same thing's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep saving, and pay off the house by about 2034. Help Sam take Joseph on as an apprentice when he's sixteen. I wouldn't change my own job unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a slow sort of anxious. It'd come and go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the children by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to have a trade and their faith. You can't automate a family sitting down to Sunday dinner. That's what I'd hold on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Would you start changing anything sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd probably still do it late. That's how I am. Sam's the one who moves, I'm the one who stays put. It's worked so far.

S4.say: Ten years is long enough to do things properly: keep apprenticeships going and keep families together. I'd want our church and town to plan for it, not wait for government.
S4.think: Ten years gets me to fifty-three, and I think I'd see it through at the plant. But even with time the same thing's coming, so I'd still be uneasy about the end.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving and pays off the house by about 2034. Helps her husband take their son on as an apprentice at sixteen, and changes her own job only if she has to.
S4.feel: A slow sort of anxiety that comes and goes.
S4.quote: You can't automate a family sitting down to Sunday dinner.
S4.fieldNote: Even with a decade, Freya's anxiety stays because the end point doesn't change. She wants the community and church to lead, not distant government. She knows she'd move late and is at peace with that, leaning on her husband as the one who adapts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is the companies keeping people on for a while, even at less pay, rather than throwing them out. And the town helping people into trades and apprenticeships, with real jobs at the end.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people still feel useful. Money's not the main thing, being needed is. If nobody needs you, what's the point of getting up at five?

headlineQuote: Money's not the main thing, being needed is.
portrait: Freya Rahman is 43, has run the wet end of a corrugator at a cardboard box plant for fifteen years, and is married to Sam, a self-employed plumber, with two children and a strong church community. She is proud of her skill, distrustful of computers and has never used AI. She's calm in a quiet future and uneasy as change comes, keeping her head down and saving. Two-year AGI alarms her because her skill and her husband's work would both be threatened, while more time lets her plan to help in Sam's business and steer their son into a family trade, though she stays anxious about the end point.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because fifteen years of skill would be made worthless with no time to change.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping people on for a while, even at less pay, and the town helping people into trades and apprenticeships with real jobs at the end.
